text.p: Israel's parliament passed the government's 1997 budget five hours into the new year Wednesday but only after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was forced to backtrack on his promise not to raise taxes.
The vote announced in the 120-seat Knesset was 60-42.

"It's a great success, an excellent budget...The time has come that we have a responsible budget, a responsible government that takes care to advance the economy along serious lines," Netanyahu told army radio.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor said the government had a full economic agenda ahead of it.

"The work is still ahead of us -- first of all to see to it that the budget is kept meticulously. Second, there are a series of reforms that we have passed already in the budget, some are still to be passed," he said.
Meridor said he now intended to work for approval of the government's Brodet committee recommendations on capital market reform proposed last October as well as tax and structural reforms.
The approximately $58.5 billion budget is supposed to contain $2.15 billion in spending cuts and new revenues in order to keep the budget deficit at 2.8 percent of gross domestic product this year.
But the Treasury still has some holes to fill after parliament earlier turned down various planned revenue-raising measures.

On Tuesday evening parliament passed the Economic Arrangements Law, which spells out legislative and other changes needed to implement the budget. Legislators agreed to reduce benefits going to newly demobilized soldiers and delay implementing a longer school day, but they rejected a Treasury plan to cancel a special half-point tax credit for working women.

Cancelling the credit would have raised $83 million the Treasury now needs to fill to meet its deficit target. Treasury officials said they would seek to fill the gap over the next few weeks with new measures.

The budget met widespread opposition in parliament, as critics charged that the brunt of the spending cuts and new revvenues would fall on the poor and disadvantaged. Meridor rescinded most of those plans.

"The average Israeli will not suffer," he said after the vote. "The standard of living will still be going up this year. I hope somewhat at a lower pace than in the past year, but the average Israeli will I hope see a change for the better."
